title: The Apocalypses and Pseudepigrapha of the Second Temple in Their Original Languages — Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, the Sibylline Oracles, 3 Baruch, the Greek Apocalypses of Moses and Esdras, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, the Apocalypse of Abraham, Hebrew Ben Sira, Aristeas, Joseph and Aseneth

license.payload: Public domain: every edition here was published before 1931 and is public domain in the United States; the texts are ancient. Internet Archive scans of public-domain volumes (Google, University of Toronto, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Graduate Theological Union and University of California copies, as each item names).

normalization: Internet Archive OCR text layers as fetched, uncorrected (text/<slug>.ocr.txt); the scan under original/<identifier>/ is the witness. The scanners read Latin, Greek and Cyrillic to varying degrees and the Syriac and Hebrew not at all: where the text layer is noise over a script, the scan is the only reading.
scope: The Second Temple apocalypses and pseudepigrapha the archive did not hold, each in the original language of its earliest surviving witness, in the standard public-domain edition. Already on the shelf and not repeated: the Septuagint deuterocanon (Judith, Tobit, 1–4 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach in Greek, Baruch, the Epistle of Jeremiah, Susanna, Bel, the Psalms of Solomon, the Odes with the Prayer of Manasseh) in EA-CORPORA-01/05; the Qumran Aramaic Enoch and Giants in EA-CORPORA-02/01; 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Ascension of Isaiah, 4 Baruch and the Ethiopic Ezra in Ge'ez in EA-CORPORA-02/20 and 20/01. 2 Enoch survives only in Slavonic; the open editions found in this pass are translations (Morfill and Charles, 1896), and Sokolov's Slavonic text (Moscow, 1910) was not found in an open scan: QUEUED. Modern critical editions (Göttingen Sirach, de Jonge's Testaments, Picard's 3 Baruch, Burchard's Aseneth) are in copyright and are not seated.

why_seated: The apocalypses between the Testaments are the archive's Revelation line before Revelation: the visions of Ezra and Baruch after the fall of the Temple, Abraham's ascent, the Sibyl's oracles, the patriarchs' last words. The Septuagint seat holds the books a canon kept; this seat holds what the canons let go, in the languages that kept them.
ruling: Lee Sharks, 2026-10-23: "detour for an ea-corpora seating. lets see. whats available of mayan texts? and then i dont think we have much or any deuterocanonical second temple lit - all those apocalypses. and what about the ethiopian canon? and euclid. all in original language or as close to it as possible. what else?" — "and the Egyptian book of the dead" — "and what about the fragments of the book of balaam?" — "yes yes yes to all - what a meal."
